new_statements.rule_in_words: Cone (Nyinpa variety) has a two-toneme system, high vs low, contrastive on the word-initial syllable; the tone of a non-initial syllable is predictable (a high first syllable spreads H rightward, HL > HH, in compounds; after a low first syllable the second is high if its vowel is short, and if long it is high after a voiceless obstruent onset and low/rising after a voiced onset, with free variation). Tone is neutralized on aspirated-onset syllables (low with a long vowel, high with a short one; high-in-isolation aspirated syllables become low when suffixed). The words 'stress' and 'prominence' (as an accentual notion) do not occur; the only 'accent' is the grave-accent diacritic marking extra-low case suffixes (p. 43). No word-stress placement is stated and stress is neither asserted nor denied.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; no stress of any kind is discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: Case markers and some verbal suffixes are always realized low and block rightward H spread (pp. 7, 43); tone not contrastive after aspirated onsets (p. 7); long-vowel second syllables with voiced onsets vary freely between H and L (p. 7); a handful of lexical exceptions to the tonogenesis rules are tabulated in section 3.1 (p. 9), where Jacques also notes that Qu (1962)'s variety assigns high tone to some syllables that are low in Nyinpa.
new_statements.identity_note: Jacques describes the Nyinpa village (Niba 尼巴, Chas.bu gshus / Cheba gou valley, southwest Cone/Zhuoni county, Gannan, Gansu) variety, from one 23-year-old consultant recorded in Chengdu in 2010; he states that the tonal system 'slightly differs from the variety of Cone Tibetan described by Qu (1962)' (preprint p. 9).

tone_statements.citation: Suzuki, Hiroyuki (鈴木博之). 2024. 下迭部チベット語洛大・代古寺[sDedgu dgon]方言の超分節音特徴 [Suprasegmental features of the sDedgu dgon dialect of Thewo-smad Tibetan]. 言語記述論集 (Journal of Kijutsuken, Descriptive Linguistics Study Group) 16: 85-106.
tone_statements.quote: 本稿で扱う sDedgu dgon 方言では、２節に示したように、調値による声調を認めない。一方で、母音の短さと発声類型による記述を提案し、理論的には、その組み合わせで計４種の超分節音的対立を形成することができるとする。... sDedgu dgon 方言のレジスターの対立は、高低レジスターの差異として記述する。レジスターは、その音声学的性質上、音節を単位として現れるが、語頭で弁別的に働くと解釈できる。... レジスターは、聴覚印象としては、発声類型よりもピッチに特徴づけられる。高レジスターが有標であり、ピッチが高めに指定され、場合によって声門の緊張が高くなる。... いずれにおいても、ピッチの相対的な高さの違いだけでは弁別に寄与しない。
tone_statements.translation: In the sDedgu dgon dialect treated here, as shown in section 2, tone defined by pitch values is not recognised. Instead a description by vowel shortness and phonation type is proposed; in theory their combination can form four suprasegmental oppositions. ... The register opposition of the sDedgu dgon dialect is described as a difference between high and low register. By its phonetic nature register appears with the syllable as its unit, but it can be interpreted as working distinctively at the beginning of the word. ... As an auditory impression, register is characterised by pitch rather than by phonation type. High register is the marked term: pitch is specified as relatively high and in some cases glottal tension increases. ... In either case, a difference in relative pitch height alone does not contribute to the distinction.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 89-90, section 3 '超分節音特徴' and 3.2 'レジスターの対立'; English abstract p. 106

tone_statements.citation: Suzuki, Hiroyuki (鈴木博之). 2022. 下迭部チベット語阿夏['Azha]方言のチベット文語形式との音対応と語彙：迭部県のチベット系諸言語の概観とともに [Sound correspondences with Written Tibetan and vocabulary of the 'Azha dialect of Thewo-smad Tibetan, with an overview of the Tibetic languages of Thewo county]. 言語記述論集 (Journal of Kijutsuken) 14: 65-114.
tone_statements.quote: ’Azha 方言には、発声類型の異なりが認められ、高低レジスターの差異として記述する 6 。高レジスターを有標とし、語頭に ˚ を付して表す。一方、低レジスターは無標である。最小対として、たとえば、˚to「投げる」と to「両/２」など。高レジスターは、声門の緊張が高くかつ高ピッチに代表される特徴をもち、時にきしみを伴う。 ... ピッチの相対的な高さは弁別に寄与せず、音節末における上昇や下降もまた弁別的ではない。レジスターは、その音声学的性質上、音節を単位として現れるが、複音節語については、最初頭の音節のレジスターが有意であると分析する 8 。
tone_statements.translation: In the ’Azha dialect a difference of phonation type is recognised, which is described as a high vs low register distinction [fn. 6]. High register is taken as marked and written with ˚ at the head of the word; low register is unmarked. A minimal pair is e.g. ˚to 'throw' vs to 'liang/two'. High register is characterised by high glottal tension and high pitch, sometimes accompanied by creak. ... Relative pitch height does not contribute to the distinction, and rises or falls at the end of the syllable are likewise not distinctive. By its phonetic nature register appears with the syllable as its unit, but for polysyllabic words the register of the very first syllable is analysed as the significant one [fn. 8].
tone_statements.locator: p. 70, sec. 2 '’Azha 方言の音体系一覧', subsection '超分節音素' with fnn. 6-8
tone_statements.summary: Two-way high vs low register contrast (high = tense glottis, high pitch, at times creaky), carried by the word's first syllable; pitch height alone and syllable-final rises/falls not distinctive.

tone_statements.citation: Chirkova, Katia. 2025. Pitch, vowel duration, and phonation in Baima and neighboring languages. Language and Linguistics 26(2): 224-261. doi:10.1075/lali.00188.chi
tone_statements.quote: Thebo and Cone, on the other hand, are analyzed as having “partial tone systems” (cf. Lin 2014: 223 for Thebo). In such a system, tone is said to be only contrastive in syllables with voiceless unaspirated obstruent and sonorant onsets (e.g. Lin 2014: 243–244 for Thebo; Jacques 2014: 284–286 for Cone) [...]. Conversely, in syllables with voiceless aspirated initials, tone is described as predictable on syllable length. It is high in short syllables and low in long syllables (as is also the case in Chos.rje). In syllables with voiced initials, on the other hand, tone is described as varying from predictably low, irrespective of vowel length (as in Cone, Jacques 2014: 285) [...]. [T]he primary division between higher-pitched and lower-pitched syllables in Thebo and Cone is likely originally associated with a tense/lax vowel distinction, induced by OT rhyme type.

tone_statements.quote: Zhuoni (Co.ne) Tibetan is spoken at Lintan County of Gannan Prefecture in Gansu Province (Qu 1962). Zhuoni appears to distinguish only two tonemes, high and low. [...] Tone splits are therefore governed by entirely different factors in Zhuoni short and long syllables. The familiar tone splitting caused by onset voicing only affected short syllables, and most long syllables, irrespective of original onset voicing, took on the low register.
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Zhuoni: secondary (Qu 1962, Qu 1988); fn 19 reduces Qu's four tones (53, 21, 55, 22) to H and L with rhyme length on the moraic tier. Long syllables generally low except those from OT syllables with non-nasal preradicals, e.g. tsh?:L <tshil> vs ka:H <skal> (p. 42). This agrees with the record (two-toneme H/L system). Tiebu (Thewo, Glottolog dialects under chon1285): first-ha

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at the stated locator in the HAL v2 PDF we hold/text (sec. 2.3, printed pp. 6-8). (2) The deciding source is a specialist's full phonological profile (preprint of the 2014 Academia Sinica chapter that Glottolog ranks first for this languoid); no better or instrumental description of Cone prosody exists per Glottolog and web search. (3) Three open sources downloaded now on another Cone dialect (Bragkhoglung: Suzuki 2012 p.3, Suzuki 2017 p.45, Zou & Suzuki 2022 pp.4-5) all describe a two-way word-tone (pitch) system with the contrast located at the word onset and say nothing of stress -- matching our 'tonal, H vs L contrastive on the first syllable, non-initial tones predictable' coding. (4) Only upgrade available is bibliographic: add the published Jacques 2014 citation alongside the preprint; no reclassification.

sources.quote: (Japanese) 'Two tones are recognised, each bearing on the word as a unit: high word-onset vs low word-onset. Only the pitch of the word onset is distinctive; whether there is a fall toward syllable/word end is not distinctive, and polysyllabic words usually show a falling intonation.' Also notes (fn. 9, p. 12) that rNam-rgyal Tshe-brtan (2008) gives no consistent description of tone. No stress/accent described.

sources.quote: Thebo and Cone, on the other hand, are analyzed as having “partial tone systems” (cf. Lin 2014: 223 for Thebo). In such a system, tone is said to be only contrastive in syllables with voiceless unaspirated obstruent and sonorant onsets (e.g. Lin 2014: 243–244 for Thebo; Jacques 2014: 284–286 for Cone) [...]. Conversely, in syllables with voiceless aspirated initials, tone is described as predictable on syllable length. It is high in short syllables and low in long syllables (as is also the case in Chos.rje). In syllables with voiced initials, on the other hand, tone is described as varying from predictably low, irrespective of vowel length (as in Cone, Jacques 2014: 285) [...]. [T]he primary division between higher-pitched and lower-pitched syllables in Thebo and Cone is likely originally associated with a tense/lax vowel distinction, induced by OT rhyme type.

sources.note: Rejects a contour/pitch-value tone analysis for sDedgu dgon (contrasting with Renzeng Wangmu 2013's five tones 55/51/54/35/12 for Rongdwangs); posits two suprasegmental distinctions: a high vs low REGISTER (high marked, higher pitch, sometimes glottal tension; distinctive on the word-initial syllable) and an independent extra-short vowel feature (falling or high-level pitch) corresponding to Written Tibetan open syllables; no minimal pairs by register alone; no word-stress statement.

tone.quote: 本稿で扱う sDedgu dgon 方言では、２節に示したように、調値による声調を認めない。一方で、母音の短さと発声類型による記述を提案し、理論的には、その組み合わせで計４種の超分節音的対立を形成することができるとする。... sDedgu dgon 方言のレジスターの対立は、高低レジスターの差異として記述する。レジスターは、その音声学的性質上、音節を単位として現れるが、語頭で弁別的に働くと解釈できる。... レジスターは、聴覚印象としては、発声類型よりもピッチに特徴づけられる。高レジスターが有標であり、ピッチが高めに指定され、場合によって声門の緊張が高くなる。... いずれにおいても、ピッチの相対的な高さの違いだけでは弁別に寄与しない。
tone.locator: pp. 89-90, section 3 '超分節音特徴' and 3.2 'レジスターの対立'; English abstract p. 106
tone.translation: In the sDedgu dgon dialect treated here, as shown in section 2, tone defined by pitch values is not recognised. Instead a description by vowel shortness and phonation type is proposed; in theory their combination can form four suprasegmental oppositions. ... The register opposition of the sDedgu dgon dialect is described as a difference between high and low register. By its phonetic nature register appears with the syllable as its unit, but it can be interpreted as working distinctively at the beginning of the word. ... As an auditory impression, register is characterised by pitch rather than by phonation type. High register is the marked term: pitch is specified as relatively high and in some cases glottal tension increases. ... In either case, a difference in relative pitch height alone does not contribute to the distinction.
tone.summary: Two registers, high (marked with ˚ before the syllable; relatively high pitch, sometimes strong glottal tension) vs low (unmarked phonation, realised at any pitch); register is word-level, significant on the first syllable, occasionally specified word-internally with no rule yet found; a second, independent suprasegmental feature 'extra-short vowel' (marked ’) realised with falling (or high-level…

tone.translation: In the ’Azha dialect a difference of phonation type is recognised, which is described as a high vs low register distinction [fn. 6]. High register is taken as marked and written with ˚ at the head of the word; low register is unmarked. A minimal pair is e.g. ˚to 'throw' vs to 'liang/two'. High register is characterised by high glottal tension and high pitch, sometimes accompanied by creak. ... Relative pitch height does not contribute to the distinction, and rises or falls at the end of the syllable are likewise not distinctive. By its phonetic nature register appears with the syllable as its unit, but for polysyllabic words the register of the very first syllable is analysed as the significant one [fn. 8].
tone.summary: Two-way high vs low register contrast (high = tense glottis, high pitch, at times creaky), carried by the word's first syllable; pitch height alone and syllable-final rises/falls not distinctive.
tone.says: Two-way high vs low register contrast (high = tense glottis, high pitch, at times creaky), carried by the word's first syllable; pitch height alone and syllable-final rises/falls not distinctive.

sources.quote: Zhuoni (Co.ne) Tibetan is spoken at Lintan County of Gannan Prefecture in Gansu Province (Qu 1962). Zhuoni appears to distinguish only two tonemes, high and low. [...] Tone splits are therefore governed by entirely different factors in Zhuoni short and long syllables. The familiar tone splitting caused by onset voicing only affected short syllables, and most long syllables, irrespective of original onset voicing, took on the low register.
sources.note: Zhuoni: secondary (Qu 1962, Qu 1988); fn 19 reduces Qu's four tones (53, 21, 55, 22) to H and L with rhyme length on the moraic tier. Long syllables generally low except those from OT syllables with non-nasal preradicals, e.g. tsh?:L <tshil> vs ka:H <skal> (p. 42). This agrees with the record (two-toneme H/L system). Tiebu (Thewo, Glottolog dialects under chon1285): first-hand data recorded by the author's student Lin Youjing in 2001 (fn 23); tone contrastive only in syllables with sonorant or voiceless unaspirated obstruent onsets, elsewhere predictable; aspirated onset

sources.note: Abstract read online: 'In these languages, it is only Cone which has a pitch distinction in its phonology. On the other hand, mBrugchu has no suprasegmentals which function in the phonology but it has a phonetically clear realisation of breathy voice'; proposes 'registrogenesis' (phonation-based registers preceding pitch), ordering mBrugchu (most phonation-like) > dPalskyid, Khodpokhog > Thewo, Sharkhog, Khromjekhog > Cone (most pitch-like).

sources.note: Describes another variety. Sharkhog Tibetan has a two-way register contrast, tense (high pitch, creaky voice) vs lax (low pitch, breathy), analysed as register rather than pitch tone; creakiness itself is not phonemic.

tone.quote: Im Tibetischen von Sharkhog erkennen wir als suprasegmental nicht die Tonhöhe, sondern das Register an. Der Grund zeigt sich in folgendem : 1. Tonhöhenwert und Tonhöhentyp sind frei. 2. Es gibt einen creaky Ton. ... können wir zwei Arten von Stimmbildung unterscheiden, und die Register „gespannt" und „locker" klassifizieren. Die Eigentümlichkeiten, die jede Gruppe begleiten, zählen sich auf wie folgt : 1. gespannt : hoher Ton, creaky Stimme, Konsonantenverbindung (teilweise), stimmlos 2. locker : tiefer Ton, breathy Stimme
tone.locator: p. 48, sec. 2.2 'Register und creaky Ton'; cf. dialect table p. 47 'Tonhöhenunterschiede.. Amdo: keine, Sharkhog: Register' and sec. 3.1 p. 52 'Aber die Spannung ist nicht phonemisch, beide werden als hohes Register beschrieben'
tone.translation: In the Tibetan of Sharkhog we recognise as the suprasegmental not pitch but register. The reason is the following: 1. Pitch value and pitch type are free. 2. There is a creaky tone. ... we can distinguish two kinds of phonation and classify the registers as 'tense' and 'lax'. The properties accompanying each group are as follows: 1. tense: high tone, creaky voice, consonant cluster (partly), voiceless 2. lax: low tone, breathy voice
tone.summary: Sharkhog Tibetan has a two-way register contrast, tense (high pitch, creaky voice) vs lax (low pitch, breathy), analysed as register rather than pitch tone; creakiness itself is not phonemic.
tone.says: Sharkhog Tibetan has a two-way register contrast, tense (high pitch, creaky voice) vs lax (low pitch, breathy), analysed as register rather than pitch tone; creakiness itself is not phonemic.
